stories.title: Common Group Unveils Goodyear Retail Center Plans
stories.excerpt: Common Bond Development Group revealed details for its latest commercial development: a premium, grocery-anchored shopping center in the master-planned community of Estrella in Goodyear, Arizona. The project brings together the City of Goodyear, developer Harvard Investments, and anchor tenant Sprouts Farmers Market to establish a new commercial heart for the trade area. Phase one of the development will total approximately 35,224 square feet, featuring a 23,024-square-foot Sprouts Farmers Market, 9,200 square feet of inline retail space, and a 3,000-square-foot standalone pad. A future second phase, situated along the lake, is planned to add 16,000 to 20,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. The center’s initial design, completed by Suite 6 Architecture + Planning incorporates a maritime theme that reflects its location on Estrella Parkway at North Lake near the Yacht Club of Estrella and the Starpointe Residents’ Club. The project is targeted to break ground in the first quarter of 2027. The post Common Group Unveils Goodyear Retail Center Plans appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Common Group breaks ground Q1 2027 on Sprouts-anchored center, Goodyear, Arizona.
Phase one: 35,224 SF retail; phase two adds 16K–20K SF restaurant/retail by lake.
Developer signals suburban retail confidence ahead of anticipated Phoenix metro population influx.
stories.summary: Common Group, Harvard Investments, and Sprouts Farmers Market are developing a grocery-anchored shopping center in Estrella, a master-planned community in Goodyear, Arizona. Phase one totals 35,224 square feet with a 23,024-SF Sprouts anchor, 9,200 SF inline retail, and a 3,000-SF pad; phase two will add 16,000–20,000 SF of retail and restaurant space along the lake. Groundbreaking is targeted for Q1 2027.
stories.impact: This Goodyear retail development signals developer confidence in sustained population growth in West Valley Phoenix suburbs. Retail anchoring precedes and validates multifamily absorption in master-planned communities; Trammell Crow should monitor Estrella's residential pipeline and absorption rates as anchor tenancy stabilizes the trade area and drives household density.

stories.title: Developer Plans 297 Housing Units Across From Downtown Brooklyn Macy’s Project
stories.excerpt: Another residential tower might be coming to Downtown Brooklyn, directly across from a major retail makeover project at the former Macy’s. Local developer Shimon Klein has filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings to bring a trio of 99-unit residential buildings along Fulton Street between Bridge and Lawrence streets. The 99-unit nature of the filing means Klein will likely try to utilize the city’s controversial 485-x tax abatement program, which comes with a construction wage requirement for projects with 100 or more units. Klein’s proposal calls for a 99-unit, 27-story building at 485 Fulton Street. The registered architect is Kao Hwa Lee from Kao Hwa Lee Architects. Neither the architect nor the developer responded to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. If approved, the building at 485 Fulton Street would have between four and eight residential units across the third through 27th floors. There would also be commercial and community facility space, as well as nearly 3,000 square feet of outdoor rooftop space for tenants. There are no further amenity details, but offerings including workout space, communal lounges, and coworking options have become non-negotiables in new residential developments. The other two 99-unit buildings would be built at 147 and 149 Lawrence Street, with similar makeups, according to the filing. The tenants of Klein’s new project would have a plethora of entertainment options in the neighborhood. The building is located across the street from 422 Fulton Street, a former Macy’s department store, which is being renovated into a five-floor retail and entertainment spot called BKX, CO previously reported. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Developer Shimon Klein files 297-unit project across from Downtown Brooklyn Macy's redevelopment.
Three 99-unit buildings on Fulton Street designed to avoid 485-x tax abatement wage requirements.
Brooklyn residential supply pipeline signals developer arbitrage on tax incentive thresholds and retail co-tenancy.
stories.summary: Local developer Shimon Klein has filed plans for three 99-unit residential buildings totaling 297 units along Fulton Street in Downtown Brooklyn, directly across from a major Macy's retail conversion. The filing strategy—splitting into three 99-unit buildings rather than one 297-unit tower—appears designed to avoid the city's 485-x tax abatement program's construction wage requirements, which apply to projects with 100+ units. The proposed 27-story building at 485 Fulton Street includes commercial and community facility space.
stories.impact: This filing reveals developer structuring to circumvent labor cost mandates in NYC, a strategy that will compress underwriting margins across the market if widely adopted. For Trammell Crow: monitor whether NYC tax abatement arbitrage erodes pro-forma returns; watch absorption and rent growth at 485 Fulton post-opening to validate Macy's redevelopment as a demand generator in Downtown Brooklyn, and assess whether competing projects will replicate Klein's threshold-avoidance filing structure.

stories.title: Wind Energy Supplier Inks Lease at Brookshire Industrial Park
stories.excerpt: Vestas-American Wind Technology leased approximately 131,300 square feet of space at Enterprise Park at Twinwood in Brookshire, Texas. The Class A industrial warehouse and office facility sits on approximately 17 acres and will support Vestas’ spare parts distribution and operations across North America. JLL’s Louis Rosenthal, Graham Horton, Cayla Wardenburg and Eric Turner represented Vestas-American Wind Technology in the transaction. Bill Gold and Faron Wiley of CBRE represented the landlord, Twinwood Industrial Owner LLC. Vestas-American Wind Technology is the North American division of Vestas, a leading provider of sustainable energy solutions and one of the world’s largest wind turbine manufacturers. The company designs, manufactures, installs and services wind energy systems. The new Brookshire facility will strengthen Vestas’ spare parts distribution network, allowing the company to better support its growing wind turbine distribution to meet demand for customers throughout the region. The post Wind Energy Supplier Inks Lease at Brookshire Industrial Park appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Vestas-American Wind Technology leases 131,300 SF at Enterprise Park, Brookshire, Texas.
Wind turbine spare parts distribution hub supports North American operations and regional demand growth.
Industrial facility lease signals green energy sector expansion and supply-chain infrastructure investment near Houston.
stories.summary: Vestas-American Wind Technology leased approximately 131,300 square feet at Enterprise Park at Twinwood in Brookshire, Texas, a Class A industrial warehouse and office facility on 17 acres. The space will serve as a spare parts distribution and operations hub for Vestas' North American wind turbine business, strengthening the company's logistics network to support growing demand.
stories.impact: This lease reflects accelerating green energy infrastructure investment in Greater Houston, which will drive sustained job and population inflow to the region. For multifamily: Vestas' commitment signals sector-specific employment clustering in industrial submarkets west of Houston; monitor population influx and wage growth in Brookshire and downstream residential demand in suburbs along I-10 west corridor.

stories.title: Avelo Airlines Reveals First McKinney National Airport Flights
stories.excerpt: McKinney National Airport’s new $79 million commercial passenger terminal is on track to start hosting flights starting in November. Avelo Airlines will launch the first-ever commercial passenger service at McKinney National Airport (DTX) on November 11, 2026. The low-cost carrier is establishing a local base with two Boeing 737 aircraft, offering nonstop flights to Las Vegas and four Florida destinations. The facility includes a 45,000-square-foot terminal with four initial gates, expanded vehicle parking, and upgraded ramp/taxiway infrastructure. Construction of the commercial terminal began in 2025. McKinney will be the third commercial airport in the DFW, along with Dallas Fort Worth International Airport and Dallas Love Field. Avelo Airlines, Inc. is an American ultra-low-cost airline headquartered in Houston, Texas. It previously operated charter flights as Casino Express Airlines and Xtra Airways before transitioning to scheduled operations and rebranding as Avelo Airlines on April 8, 2021. The post Avelo Airlines Reveals First McKinney National Airport Flights appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: McKinney National Airport opens $79M commercial terminal November 2026; Avelo Airlines launch anchor tenant.
Two Boeing 737 aircraft base with nonstop service to Las Vegas and four Florida destinations.
Third DFW commercial airport signals North Texas air-hub growth and residential demand catalyst in McKinney.
stories.summary: McKinney National Airport's new $79 million, 45,000-square-foot commercial passenger terminal is on track to open in November 2026, with Avelo Airlines launching the airport's first scheduled service. Avelo will base two Boeing 737 aircraft at the facility, offering nonstop flights to Las Vegas and four Florida destinations. The airport will be the third commercial aviation hub in the DFW metroplex alongside DFW International and Dallas Love Field.
stories.impact: Commercial aviation service creates a demand catalyst for multifamily growth in McKinney and surrounding North Dallas suburbs by improving business-travel accessibility and attracting corporate relocation. Trammell Crow should front-run residential development in McKinney's northeast quadrant and evaluate whether air-service activation justifies higher rents and density in airport-proximate submarkets; monitor Fortune 500 relocation announcements to DFW in 2026–2027.

stories.title: Spirit Airlines Dania Beach HQ Sells at Auction for $93.25M
stories.excerpt: Spirit Airlines’ shuttered headquarters building in Dania Beach was acquired at auction for $93.25 million. A Hill City Capital affiliate was the buyer of the office campus, totaling over 600,000 square feet. The facility was delivered just two years ago. The campus covered more than 11 acres and comprised four buildings, including corporate offices, an amenity building, a crew-training facility with flight simulators and corporate housing. The low-cost carrier shut down abruptly on May 2 after a last-minute bailout from the federal government failed to materialize. About 17,000 employees lost their jobs. With the airline no longer operating, its bankruptcy estate began monetizing its remaining assets. That includes aircraft, equipment, airport-related assets and real estate. Hill City Capital is a Boston-based investment firm and hedge fund founded in 2020. It manages roughly $4.9 billion in discretionary assets focusing on concentrated, long-biased equity strategies within sectors like industrials, transportation, and business services The post Spirit Airlines Dania Beach HQ Sells at Auction for $93.25M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Spirit Airlines shuttered HQ campus sold at auction for $93.25M; Hill City Capital buyer.
600K+ SF office campus on 11 acres, delivered two years prior, now monetized via bankruptcy.
Dania Beach office asset fire-sale signals aviation sector distress and flight from speculative office development.
stories.summary: Spirit Airlines' headquarters campus in Dania Beach, Florida was acquired at auction for $93.25 million by Hill City Capital, a Boston-based hedge fund. The 600,000+ square-foot office campus, delivered just two years ago, sits on 11 acres and includes corporate offices, amenity building, crew-training facility, and corporate housing. Spirit shut down abruptly on May 2 after a failed federal bailout, resulting in 17,000 job losses and asset liquidation via bankruptcy.
stories.impact: Spirit's collapse and fire-sale of a newly-built office campus underscores catastrophic headwinds in aviation labor and low-cost carrier economics, with spillover risk to regional employment hubs. For Trammell Crow in South Florida: this signals localized job destruction and potential residential rent compression in Dania Beach and Fort Lauderdale; monitor whether Hill City's acquisition signals office-to-alternative-use conversion (data center, logistics, mixed-use) that might regenerate employment and stabilize regional multifamily demand.

stories.title: Payments Manager Corpay Cross-Border Relocates to 18K SF at 560 Lexington Avenue
stories.excerpt: An international payment and currency risk management firm is planning a headquarters relocation to Rudin’s 560 Lexington Avenue. Corpay Cross-Border Solutions, which operates under corporate payments company Corpay, has signed an 11-year lease for 17,778 square feet at the Plaza District tower, Commercial Observer has learned. The landlord declined to provide the asking rent, but an April lease inside Rudin’s 22-story tower asked $84 per square foot, according to previous CO reports. Jacob Rosenthal and Kevin Carroll of CBRE represented Corpay, while Rudin was represented in-house by Kevin Daly and a CBRE team of Peter Turchin, Brett Shannon, Eric Deutsch and Lauren Levy. Corpay Cross-Border plans to move from Tishman Speyer‘s 300 Park Avenue into its new, prebuilt office, which occupies the entire 17th floor of 560 Lexington, this fall. Daly, Rudin’s vice president of office leasing, stated that the deal validates recent portfolio investments, which allowed for minimal modifications to meet Corpay’s space requirements. “This allowed us to accommodate their accelerated timeline for move-in, which was a big factor in getting the deal done,” Daly said. Located two blocks from Grand Central Terminal, the 380,000-square-foot office building at the corner of Lexington Avenue and East 50th Street has seen over 91,000 square feet of leasing activity in the last six months, according to Rudin. Recent arrivals include financial firm Marex, hedge fund SummitTX and coworking firm Industrious. Spokespeople for CBRE and Corpay Cross-Border did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Corpay Cross-Border Solutions leases 17,778 SF at 560 Lexington Avenue, Manhattan, 11-year term.
Relocates from Tishman Speyer's 300 Park Avenue; rent ~$84/SF indicates Plaza District office strength.
International payments firm HQ consolidation reflects office demand stabilization in Midtown Manhattan post-pandemic.
stories.summary: Corpay Cross-Border Solutions, an international payments and currency risk management firm, has signed an 11-year lease for 17,778 square feet at Rudin's 560 Lexington Avenue in Midtown Manhattan's Plaza District. The firm is relocating from Tishman Speyer's 300 Park Avenue and will occupy the entire 17th floor. Asking rent was approximately $84 per square foot, and the move is scheduled for fall 2024.
stories.impact: This Plaza District lease validates office market recovery in core Midtown Manhattan and signals tenant confidence in long-term office occupancy and lease terms. For Trammell Crow: office-market stabilization in Manhattan increases residential demand from white-collar workers securing multi-year office tenancy; monitor whether similar financial-services consolidations drive residential absorption in Midtown-proximate neighborhoods (Kips Bay, Murray Hill, Gramercy) and support rent growth in luxury and Class A multifamily stock.

stories.title: Charlotte Apartments Trade for $76.3M
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer made its first foray into the Charlotte market, purchasing Berkshire Dilworth, a 296-unit luxury multifamily property between West Midtown and the historic Dilworth neighborhood. Berkshire Residential was the seller of the asset, which traded for $76.3 million, or just over $250,000 a unit. Berkshire Dilworth, located at 1351 E. Morehead St., is 97 percent occupied. The unit mix includes studios and one- to three-bedroom floorplans with an average size of 856 square feet. Interior amenities at Berkshire Dilworth comprise a 24-hour fitness center, a yoga studio, a resident lounge, coworking spaces, a clubhouse and a rooftop lounge with a fireplace. Outdoor offerings include a swimming pool, a sundeck and a terrace lounge. The community also includes 3,000 square feet of street-level retail. Tishman Speyer is planning to upgrade the property’s amenities and exterior, along with select apartment improvements. Newmark’s John Heimburger, Dean Smith and Sean Wood represented Berkshire Residential. The post Charlotte Apartments Trade for $76.3M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Tishman Speyer acquires Berkshire Dilworth, 296-unit luxury apartments, Charlotte for $76.3M ($257.8K/unit).
97% occupied; 856-SF average unit; located between West Midtown and historic Dilworth neighborhood.
Institutional investor entry into Charlotte market signals confidence in Sunbelt multifamily fundamentals and rent growth.
stories.summary: Tishman Speyer purchased Berkshire Dilworth, a 296-unit luxury multifamily property in Charlotte, North Carolina, for $76.3 million, or approximately $257,800 per unit. The asset, located at 1351 E. Morehead Street between West Midtown and the historic Dilworth neighborhood, is 97% occupied with studios and one- to three-bedroom units averaging 856 square feet. Tishman Speyer plans amenity and exterior upgrades, plus selective unit improvements.
stories.impact: Tishman Speyer's entry into Charlotte signals institutional investor conviction in the market's rent-growth fundamentals and Sunbelt migration tailwinds. For Trammell Crow: the $257.8K/unit valuation sets a market comp for Charlotte Class A multifamily; monitor cap-rate compression and whether similar institutional acquisitions indicate headroom for new development starts, particularly in West Midtown and surrounding transit-accessible submarkets experiencing demographic influx and income growth.

stories.title: John McCullough of Kennedy Wilson Multifamily Development: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Since joining Kennedy Wilson following the firm’s $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers’ apartment living platform in 2025, John McCullough has been serving as president of the real estate investment company’s multifamily development group, where he oversees every aspect of the firm’s U.S. development business. Kennedy Wilson’s acquisition of Toll Brothers’ platform gave it general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties, with assets under management of $2.2 billion. The firm also purchased a pipeline of 29 development sites in various stages of construction. Toll Brothers’ entire apartment living management team has transitioned over to Kennedy Wilson under the leadership of McCullough, who previously led apartment living operations at Toll Brothers. But McCullough’s real estate path wasn’t always laid out for him, as he started out in the U.S. Navy and then eventually hit his business stride at school in Boston. Commercial Observer caught up with McCullough last month to discuss his entry into real estate, the Toll Brothers acquisition, and his mission at Kennedy Wilson. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: How’d you get started in real estate? John McCullough: I got started in real estate in a roundabout way. I went to the United States Naval Academy for my undergrad, and graduated in 1994, and then served five years in what we would refer to as the surface navy. If I had stayed in the Navy long-term, I would have trained to be the captain of a ship. I served on two large aircraft carriers out in San Diego, and it was a great experience. It was a really good grounding in the fundamentals of leadership I was put into a lot of situations that were incredibly difficult as a 23- or 24-year-old, but I learned a lot from that. bullets: Kennedy Wilson acquires Toll Brothers apartment platform for $347M; 18 properties, $2.2B AUM.
John McCullough (ex-Toll COO) leads 29-site development pipeline and management team transition.
Major platform consolidation signals capital concentration and operational scaling in multifamily development segment.
stories.summary: Kennedy Wilson acquired Toll Brothers' entire apartment living platform for $347 million, gaining general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties with $2.2 billion in assets under management and a pipeline of 29 development sites. stories.impact: This platform acquisition consolidates a major development pipeline under institutional capital and experienced management, accelerating project velocity and potentially compressing market timelines for competitive entries. For Trammell Crow: track Kennedy Wilson's 29-site pipeline by market and stage; anticipate accelerated deliveries in 2026–2028 that may compress rent growth and cap rates in overlapping markets; assess whether the Toll platform's geographic footprint (likely Sunbelt and high-growth metros) overlaps with Trammell Crow's acquisition targets.

stories.title: Southern Land Company Hires Tony Marchbanks as Head of Homebuilding
stories.excerpt: Southern Land Company has made a leadership hire to spearhead single-family home development in three key states, Commercial Observer has learned. Tony Marchbanks has joined the firm as national president of homebuilding, in which he will focus not only on the U.S., but also focus particularly on Tennessee, Texas and Colorado, according to Southern Land. Marchbanks brings with him 30 years of real estate experience and most recently served as chief operating officer for Highland Homes, where he launched a building spree in the Houston market, producing 1,000 homes per year, Southern Land said. “Higher interest rates and lack of job growth all culminate into a lack of consumer confidence, so you have all three key contributors to a good homebuilding environment that are headwinds at this time,” Marchbanks told CO. “But for a company like Southern Land, it’s actually a huge opportunity because they have expansion plans, particularly into Texas, which is the largest new home market in the country,” Marchbanks said. “Most builders secured their lot supply three years ago, and now they have too many lots. So it’s an opportunity for a company like Southern Land to find and [invest] in communities they wouldn’t have been able to in a strong market.” Southern Land is currently developing four master-planned communities across 5,000 individual lots in its portfolio. Marchbanks will oversee the construction, purchasing, sales and architecture for those soon-to-be neighborhoods. Southern Land has been making some changes in recent months by launching its own mortgage lending division in May to augment its sales division and support its construction pipeline, CO reported at the time. Build-to-sell homes are not the only residential asset class Southern Land has been dabbling in either, as it builds multifamily properties in Las Vegas; Erie, Colo.; and just outside Austin, Tex. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Southern Land Company hires Tony Marchbanks (ex-Highland Homes COO) as national president of homebuilding.
Marchbanks built 1,000 homes/year in Houston; now targets Tennessee, Texas, Colorado expansion.
Experienced homebuilder exec signals Southern Land's lot-supply advantage in tight new-home market consolidation.
stories.summary: Southern Land Company hired Tony Marchbanks as national president of homebuilding, focusing on single-family development in Tennessee, Texas, and Colorado. Marchbanks previously served as COO of Highland Homes, where he oversaw production of 1,000 homes per year in Houston. Marchbanks noted that while interest rates and weak job growth challenge the sector, Southern Land's lot supply positions the firm to capture market share from competitors holding excess inventory.
stories.impact: Marchbanks' hire signals Southern Land's competitive positioning via lot-supply arbitrage in a constrained new-home market; higher rates and weak consumer confidence favor land-rich incumbents over leverage-dependent builders. For Trammell Crow: monitor whether single-family oversupply in Texas and Colorado compresses household formation and rental demand in those markets; assess whether Southern Land's expansion accelerates lot velocity and pricing, thereby constraining multifamily sites' land costs in overlapping Texas markets.

stories.title: How Trent Johnson, Brian Landrum at Harbert Management Corp. Invest in Senior Housing
stories.excerpt: Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum are senior managing directors and co-heads of the seniors housing team at Harbert Management Corporation, an $8 billion alternatives asset management firm founded in 1993. The group has been investing in the seniors housing space for 15 years, raising a $210 million investment fund in 2016 and a $510 million investment fund for the space in 2020. The group is currently on its third fundraise, as they attempt to capitalize on the first wave of Baby Boomers turning 80-years-old in 2016. The duo sat down with Commercial Observer to discuss their careers, how the asset class has evolved, the present and future of the senior housing space, and where the best investment opportunities will be in an increasingly important asset class. (This conversation has been edited for length and clarity) Commercial Observer: How long have you been involved in the senior housing space? Trent Johnson: I started investing in the space in 2012, which is where I met Brian at Fortress Investment Group. I actually came from a legal background. I started out as a real estate lawyer, and then I spent a lot of years at an apartment investment and management company, which was a large multifamily REIT based out of Denver, Colo, Apartment Investment and Management Company. I was recruited away to start and lead a seniors housing platform in Dallas, which is where I joined forces with Brian, and we co-headed that office here in Dallas. Brian Landrum: I started investing in seniors housing in 2009 at a predecessor firm, Walton Street Capital, which was a diversified real estate private equity firm, and then in 2012, I joined forces with Trent in 2012 at Fortress Investment Group, which is where we began working together, and then ultimately, made a decision to join up at Harbert Management Corporation in 2015. Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum co-lead team; third fundraise underway to capitalize on Baby Boomer aging.
Institutional capital targeting first wave of Baby Boomers turning 80 in 2016; sector fundamentals strengthening.

Co-heads Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum are currently executing a third fundraise to capture the first wave of Baby Boomers turning 80, beginning in 2016. The interview explores career paths, asset-class evolution, and emerging investment opportunities in seniors housing.
stories.impact: Institutional capital concentration in seniors housing reflects demographic conviction and capital deployment ahead of peak Baby Boomer aging curves (2025–2035). For Trammell Crow: monitor Harbert's deployment geography and acquisition strategy to identify competing multifamily submarkets where seniors housing competes for land and capital; assess whether seniors housing cap rates and returns are attracting capital away from conventional multifamily, potentially reducing development competition in certain markets while intensifying it in age-dense Sunbelt metros (Florida, Arizona, Carolinas).
